11502-an-englishman-looks-at-the-world-b:
H. G. Wells's 1914 Englishman Looks at the World gathers unrestrained remarks on contemporary matters in twenty-six essays. Starting with Blériot's flight and its consequences for cheap travel, Wells considers the king and a new epoch, empire, labour unrest, socialism, modern warfare, the novel. the public library, Chesterton and Belloc, Sir Thomas More, London traffic, sociology, divorce, schoolmasters, motherhood, doctors, specialization, parliaments, American population, civilizational collapse, and the ideal citizen.

Wells writes as a prophet of the new age, confident and combative. The collection shows Edwardian progressive thought just before the war tested it. Readers of Wells's nonfiction will find here his breadth: aviation, politics, literature, and social reform in one restless volume.
11890-comrades-of-the-saddle-or-the-youn:
Frank V. Webster's 1910 boys' book, subtitled The Young Rough Riders of the Plains, follows a group of young riders on the western plains. Webster, already known for school and farm stories such as Only a Farm Boy and Tom the Telephone Boy, writes for readers who liked horses, camps, and quick action.

Chapters show the boys packing saddle bags with food, plates, coffee, and blankets, buckling on cartridge belts, and riding out with rifles across their shoulders. Talk of ranch deals and bragging heard in El Paso gives the adventure a plot beyond the trail, as the riders test themselves against older men who doubt them.
13603-the-hawaiian-romance-of-laieikawai:
Martha Warren Beckwith gives the Hawaiian romance of Laieikawai with introduction and translation, illustrated by a kahuna or native sorcerer. Conclusions, persons, action, and background precede text and translation, from the princess's birth and flight to Paliuli through wooing, boxing, and the house thatched with bird feathers.

Aiwohikupua goes to woo the princess, deserts his sisters, and meets the guardians of Paliuli, while Kahalaomapuana. The princess's war chief, warns Hauailiki to go back or birds of Paliuli will eat his flesh. Hauailiki flees to Keaau by early morning. Beckwith preserves a Hawaiian chiefly romance in both languages, with scholarship that lets English readers follow its gods, chiefs, and customs.
16233-an-essay-towards-fixing-the-true-s:
First printed in 1744 and reprinted in 1947 by the Augustan Reprint Society, this essay tries to fix true standards for wit, humor, raillery, satire, and ridicule. James L. Clifford supplies an introduction and a bibliographical note, placing the short work among eighteenth-century debates about taste. The Augustan editors present it as a text worth study, priced at one dollar.

Its opening pages tease the flattery of dedications, noting that writers in dedications, like carvers of tomb inscriptions, seldom tell hard truths. The essay then sorts kinds of comic writing with Augustan care for definition. Students of satire, rhetoric, and eighteenth-century letters will find a compact, witty specimen.
20184-the-adventures-of-uncle-jeremiah-a:
Uncle Jeremiah and his family visit the great fair in this comic tale. He rides in comfort and marvels at the age of travel. All nations feed our appetites, he says in wonder and pride. Millions are spent to carry us in ease, he tells a stranger.

He travels with Sarah and Mary's two children toward the fair. Great fairs drew farm families to gape at machines, foods, and nations. The tale turns their wonder into gentle, folksy comedy throughout. Readers get a period snapshot of rural folk meeting the modern world.
21319-three-boys-or-the-chiefs-of-the-cl:
A nearly ruined castle on Scotland's northwest coast houses the chiefs of the Clan Mackhai in George Manville Fenn's tale. Max, a London lawyer's son, is sent to stay there because the chief has borrowed heavily from Max's father and not repaid. The chief's son Kenneth and his gillie put Max through test after test of bravery.

Slaps, kicks, and Highland tempers fly from the first chapter, with young Scoodrach caught between the boys. Behind the sport sits real money trouble: the castle itself is under threat of seizure for debt. Fenn mixes peril after peril with clan pride, and the end follows plainly once Max learns what his visit means.
25708-the-hero-of-ticonderoga-or-ethan-a:
John De Morgan writes this boys' history tale, The Hero of Ticonderoga, or Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys, published in Philadelphia by David McKay in 1896. De Morgan, author of Paul Revere and The First Shot for Liberty, fronts the book with a wallet drawn silently by a stick.

Chapters open at the courthouse, with the Green Mountain Boys, a child of nature, and the rising of the moon. Defiance, an ambuscade, a convention, and treachery follow. Zeb's double dealing and the tables turned lead to war, Benedict Arnold, and the hero of Ticonderoga itself, with Crown Point and news from Boston.
4068-froudacity-west-indian-fables-by-ja:
A reply to James Anthony Froude's West Indian fables, prefaced by J. J. Thomas, answers the historian's account of the islands. The book follows Froude's voyage out through Barbados, St. Vincent, and Grenada, then turns to Trinidad and its struggle for political enfranchisement.

Thomas argues that Froude's scheme for future rule arrived out of season, and that the gentlemen of Trinidad would meet his historical self-praise with indignant contempt. The work is a sharp colonial rebuttal, written in 1888's heat. Readers interested in Caribbean history will find a direct, angry answer to an imperial traveler.
6094-the-scouts-of-stonewall-the-story-o:
Joseph A. Altsheler continues his Civil War series with The Scouts of Stonewall, the story of the Great Valley campaign. Though an independent story, it follows The Guns of Bull Run and The Guns of Shiloh, reverting to the Southern side and the fortunes of Harry Kenton and his friends.

Harry fights for the South while his cousin Dick Mason fights for the North, with Colonel Kenton, Mrs. Mason, Juliana, and officers of both armies around them. Later volumes carry the series to Antietam, Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Appomattox. Altsheler writes boy-centered war romance with maps of loyalty and kin.
7777-narrative-of-the-voyages-round-the-:
Andrew Kippis tells the life of Captain James Cook in this narrative of his voyages round the world, with an account of his years between voyages. Dedicated to the king, it credits royal patronage with making Cook's vast undertakings possible, and with throwing new light on geography, navigation, and science.

The book follows Cook from early service to Pacific discovery, praising a reign that backed learning as well as empire. Through journals, letters, and plain narration, it presents a navigator whose charts and findings reshaped how Britain saw the globe, and whose name became tied to exploration itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abisai:
Abisai, Sarvia's son, Joab's brother, and David's nephew, stands in this entry as one of David's most valiant warriors and most faithful friends. He fought beside David against Saul, then against the Ammonites, Syrians, and Edomites, and later against Absalom, Seba, and the Philistines. The entry follows him through Samuel and Chronicles, marking each campaign with its passage.

His loyalty shows most sharply in the hard moments, when he backs David against rebels and foreign armies alike. The record is short and built almost entirely from scripture citations, with references to Hagen, Palis, and White for readers who want the scholarly background. It presents a soldier defined less by his own story than by steadfast service to his king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adonai:
Adonai, Hebrew for lord or ruler, is a name bestowed on God in the Old Testament, kept in the Vulgate and its dependent versions, at Exodus 6:3 and Judith 16:16. No other name for God is more definite or more easily understood. Etymologically it pluralizes Adon, with the first-person singular possessive suffix.

This plural has drawn various explanations. As a plurale abstractum it would signal the fullness of divine sway, pointing to God as Lord of lords, an explanation Hebrew grammarians endorse, distinguishing a plurale virium or virtutum. Others prefer plurale excellentiae, magnitudinis, or majestatis. It is not a politeness form like German Sie or French vous, and the possessive adds no more meaning than in Rabbi, Monsieur, or Madonna. Adonai also perpetually substitutes for the ineffable name Yahve, lending it vowel signs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aggeus-haggai:
Aggeus, tenth among the Old Testament minor prophets, is called Haggay in Hebrew and Haggaios in the Septuagint, whence Latin Aggeus. His name's meaning is uncertain. Many scholars read it as the festive one, born on a feast day. Others take it as short for Haggiyyah, my feast is Yahweh, a name found in Chronicles.

His personal life is equally uncertain. His book is very short and gives no detail about its author. Its few passages speak only of his divine message delivered in Jerusalem in the second year of Darius I, 520 BC. Jewish tradition, judged to have little historical basis, says he was born in Chaldea during the Captivity, came young to Jerusalem with returning exiles, and was buried among the priests. He has also been wrongly credited with Psalms 111 and 145.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-mai:
Angelo Mai, Roman cardinal and celebrated philologist, was born at Schilpario in Bergamo in 1782 and died at Albano in 1854. Young, he entered the Society of Jesus, was sent to Naples in 1804, and was stationed at Orvieto and Rome. For his skill in palaeography he was appointed in 1811 to the Ambrosian Library at Milan.

This led to his initial discoveries in palimpsests, old manuscripts washed and written over. He found Cicero's orations in 1814 and the correspondence of Fronto, Marcus Aurelius, and Verus in 1815. A speech of Isaeus and a fragment of Plautus's Vidularia followed in 1816, with a Gothic Saint Paul in 1817. He later printed unpublished pages of more than 350 authors, including Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Origen, and Italian humanists. After long delays he published the Vatican codex, an important Greek Bible manuscript, in 1858. The gall nut he used to revive palimpsest writings half destroyed them, though all reagents injure parchment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-odo-o: Odo of Cambrai, a teacher turned Benedictine abbot and bishop, won fame at Tournai before his stormy tenure at Cambrai. Invited to teach there in 1087, he became a monk in 1095 and abbot of Saint Martin's, then Bishop of Cambrai, consecrated at Reims. Refusing investiture from Emperor Henry IV delayed his possession of the see. Though Henry's son restored it in 1106, Odo was exiled in 1110 and died at Anchin in 1113 without regaining it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cambrai:
Cambrai covers the whole French department of Nord. Before 1559 it was a bishopric of huge reach, taking in even Brussels and Antwerp. The new metropolis of Malines and eleven other dioceses cut it down, and by way of compensation it became an archbishopric with Saint Omer, Tournai, and Namur under it. The Concordat of 1802 reduced it again to a bishopric under Paris.

On Bishop Belmas's death in 1841 it rose once more to an archbishopric, with Arras as suffragan. Its bishops run from Saint Vedulphus, on whose death in 580 the residence moved from Arras to Cambrai. Later names include Saint Gaugericus, Halitgarius, apostle of the Danes, Gerard the Great, who converted the Gondulphian heretics, and Robert of Geneva, antipope in 1378 as Clement VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chusai:
An entry on Chusai the Archite, native of Archi south of Ephraim near Bethel, called in Chronicles the king's friend. That title, like counsellor for Ahitophel or army leader for Joab, was an official rank among the Seleucids for trusted men with military or civil duties, not mere intimacy. In Chusai's case, however, the story of Absalom's rebellion shows the title was more than official.

Just after David learned of Ahitophel's treason, Chusai met him on the Mount of Olives, garments torn and head dusted. David, judging the old man a burden in flight, sent him to Jerusalem to defeat Ahitophel's counsel. Chusai won Absalom's trust, and in council he secured a delay that saved the king, then sent word to David through Zadok, Abiathar, and their sons. Scripture reports his deception without approving it, and the entry asks how far war's ethics can justify it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctrine-of-a:
The Doctrine of Addai is a Syriac document telling the legend of the conversion of Edessa. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with King Abgar's letter to Christ and the reply, which here is a spoken message with a portrait of Christ, not a letter as Eusebius has it. After the Ascension, Thomas dispatched Addai, counted among the seventy-two disciples, to heal the king and preach at his court.

Addai told of the True Cross found by Protonice, wife of the emperor Claudius, a tale later than Eusebius and built on the story of Saint Helena. The people were converted, and the heathen altars fell. The entry weighs the document's sources and dates, giving readers a window onto the legends of the earliest Syrian church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-douai:
Douai, a town and former university seat in France's Nord department, stands on the River Scarpe, about twenty miles south of Lille. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts about thirty thousand people and notes its strong old ramparts, removed only in recent years. Medieval Douai thrived, and its church of Notre-Dame goes back to the twelfth century.

To English Catholics the name is bound to the college founded by Cardinal Allen under Elizabeth, where most of the clergy were trained in penal times. To that college England owed much of the survival of its Catholic faith. Scots and Irish colleges, with Benedictine and Franciscan houses, joined it, and the entry lists their histories for the reader.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesychius-of-:
Hesychius of Sinai was a Byzantine priest and monk of the Thorn-bush monastery on Mount Sinai and an ascetic author now almost forgotten. Nothing definite is known of his career or the exact time he lived, and only a few fragments of his writings survive, still awaiting collection and separate criticism. In manuscripts he usually bears the honorary title Our Holy Father, which helps tell him apart from other men of the same name.

The key test for his work lies in his Bible quotations, which regularly follow the Codex Sinaiticus, unlike the version used by his namesake of Jerusalem. The pivotal piece is a collection of two hundred ascetic maxims on watchfulness and virtue, printed under the Jerusalem Hesychius in Migne's edition. The entry shows how much of that edition can only be assigned by close monographic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-mo:
Jacques de Molai, also spelled Molay, was born at Rahon, Jura, about 1244. He died at Paris on 18 March 1314. A Templar at Beaune since 1265, he appears as grand master as early as 1298. At trial he called himself an unlettered soldier. Yet he drew on his order's collective experience to preside in 1306 or 1307 over a major crusade plan. He carried it to Poitiers for Clement V, who had summoned him from the East.

Renan judged that plan, built on firsthand knowledge of the Orient and Italian cities, superior to any rival scheme of its age. In it Molai showed full trust in France's king, who soon became his destroyer. At the same time he gave the pope a memorial against merging Hospitallers and Templars, a union debated since Lyons council. The entry presents a soldier-statesman on the eve of his order's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-nicolai:
Jean Nicolai, a celebrated French Dominican theologian born at Mouzay in 1594 and dead in Paris in 1673. He entered his order at twelve, professed in 1612, and took a Sorbonne doctorate in 1632. He taught philosophy and theology with distinction in many houses, prized for strict observance, prudence, erudition, and penetration.

Nicolai knew Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish, and Hebrew, sat on the commission examining Jansenist works, and held strictly to Thomist teaching on grace against the Molinists. His books fall in three groups: annotated editions of older theologians, his own theology, and verse and political pieces. Against Jansenists he added a dissertation to each volume of his Pantheologia edition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molokai:
Molokai, fifth in size among Hawaii's main islands, lies between Oahu and Maui. It is a rugged volcanic island about thirty-eight miles long and seven wide. Cliffs up to 3,500 feet fringe its northern shore. Annexed by the United States in 1898, it counted 2,504 people in the 1900 census. Grazing filled its southern slopes, and a coral reef lined the south coast.

Worldwide fame came through its leper settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula. Father Damien arrived to stay in 1873 and brought order and energy to a struggling community. Franciscan sisters from Syracuse followed in the 1880s. The entry also covers water supply works and the settlement's shift from Kalawao to Kalaupapa. It notes the island's honey, deer and torrent streams.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shammai:
Shammai, called the Elder, was a famous Jewish scribe who, with Hillel, formed the last of the pairs who led the Sanhedrin. Their schools held rival sway, by Talmudic tradition, from about a century before Jerusalem's destruction in 70 AD. The Mishna, the only trustworthy authority here, mentions Shammai in just eight passages. Little else is known with certainty about either great scribe. In character and teaching, Shammai was Hillel's opposite in every way.

He lived the law to the letter with stern severity, pressing legal interpretation to an extreme. The tale is told that when his daughter-in-law bore a child on the feast of Tabernacles, he had the roof broken through. The bed was roofed with boughs, so the infant might keep the feast in a makeshift booth. The strictness of the master marked his school against Hillel's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-tour:
Simon of Tournai taught at the University of Paris at the start of the 1200s, with birth and death dates unknown. He was teaching before 1184, since he signed a document alongside Gerard de Pucelle, who died Bishop of Coventry that year. Chroniclers agree on his brilliance in philosophy, which he taught for ten years. Later he lectured on theology with equal success, drawing on Aristotle and other works newly known through Arab translators.

His teachings drew suspicion by the end of the 1100s. Enemies, likely foes of the new philosophy, spread accounts by Thomas de Cantimpré, Matthew Paris, and Giraldus Cambrensis. They differ in detail but agree that Simon was struck dumb for blasphemy or heretical claims. Whether he said in private more than his works contain is now hard to judge. His surviving works, few printed, are orthodox, including a Summa and Sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinai:
Sinai is the mountain where the Mosaic Law was given. Jerome and Gesenius treated Horeb and Sinai as one name, while Ewald, Robinson, and Palmer held Horeb for the whole region around Sinai. The name's origin is disputed, whether from a Hebrew word for desert or for the moon god. The mount was called Sinai, or the mount of God, probably before Moses's day.

The name now covers the triangular peninsula between southern Palestine's desert, the Red Sea, and the gulfs of Aqaba and Suez. It spans about 10,000 square miles, scene of Israel's forty years of wandering after the Exodus. North of Jabal et-Tih stretches an arid plateau cut by wadis, including El-Arish, the River of Egypt. South rises a granite mass split into three groups, western Serbal, central Musa, Catherine, and Um Schomer, and eastern Thebt, peopled by semi-nomadic Arab Muslims under tribal sheikhs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-of-to:
Stephen of Tournai, a canonist, wrote a Summa on Gratian's Decretum that shaped medieval church law. An Orléans man born in 1128, he joined the regular canons of Saint-Euverte there about 1150. He learned canon and Roman law at Bologna and came home to his house in 1160. The canons chose him abbot of Saint-Euverte in 1167, and Paris's Sainte-Geneviève chose him in 1177.

The Paris monastery he almost entirely rebuilt, founding a monastic school beside it. In 1192 he became bishop of Tournai, but popular opposition and the interdict on France over Philip II's divorce proceedings hampered him greatly. His Summa in decretum Gratiani of 1159 draws heavily on Paucapalea, Rufinus, and Rolandus, the future Alexander III, and was first edited by Schulte at Giessen in 1891. His letters fill pages 309 to 625 of volume 111 of the Patrology. He died at Tournai in September 1203.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tournai:
Tournai is a diocese in Belgium, evangelized by St. Piat in the later third century, though he cannot be proved its first bishop. Piat suffered martyrdom under Maximian, and barbarian invasions then wiped out Christian life in the region until the Franks came. Clodion settled at Tournai, Childeric died there in 481, and St. Remigius used Frankish goodwill to organize the northern hierarchy.

Remigius erected the see of Tournai about 500, naming Eleutherius as its bishop. It kept its own bishops for nearly a century, then about 626 its see joined Noyon under one bishop, a union lasting five hundred years. In 1559 Philip II split the vast diocese, taking nearly two-thirds of its land for the new sees of Bruges and Ghent, with six parishes to Ypres. After the Revolution its bounds matched the province of Hainault.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-upper-kassai:
Upper Kassai began as a simple mission in 1901 and was detached as a prefecture apostolic from the Vicariate of Belgian Congo on 20 August 1901. The prefect apostolic lived at the mission of St Joseph de Luluabourg, a few miles south of the Belgian station of Luluabourg. That mission lay in the Lualaba-Kassai district, whose chief town Lusambo housed the district commissioner. At its creation the prefecture covered almost the whole district.

Its bounds ran from the Vicariate of Belgian Congo in the north and east to Portuguese Congo in the south and the Lubue river in the west. In 1908 it grew eastward to the left bank of the Lualaba and westward to a new line. The entry lists its stations, priests, and schools, a brief administrative record of a mission district taking shape in the Belgian Congo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zarai:
Zarai is the Numidian titular see named in the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table. Ptolemy calls it Zaratha and wrongly places it in Mauretania Caesariensis; it is probably Apuleius's Zaratha too. The forms Zaratha and Zaraitani, found in inscriptions, suggest the name Zarai on another inscription lost a final dental letter. Its ruins, Henshir Zaria, southeast of Setif in Algeria, crown a height commanding the left bank of the Oued Taourlatent, which medieval Arabs called Oued Zaraoua.

Remains of a Byzantine citadel and two Christian basilicas are still visible there. Only two bishops of Zarai are known: Cresconius, present at Carthage's conference in 411 against the Donatist rival Rogatus. Adeodatus, exiled by Huneric after Carthage's conference in 484, died in exile for the faith. The entry draws on Smith's Greek and Roman geography, Müller's notes on Ptolemy, Toulotte's Christian Africa, and Diehl's Byzantine Africa.
doe-osti-2589582-machine-learning-models: Machine learning for PDE optimization got its DOE models, and this LDRD report covers the constrained approach. The pages detail the methods. The computational folks get their briefing. The report was LDRD. The optimization was PDE constrained. The folks were computational.
doe-osti-3006734-fair-surrogate-benchmar: FAIR surrogate benchmarks got their DOE final, and this report supports AI research. The pages detail the findings. The AI folks get their closeout. The benchmarks were surrogate. The closeout was AI. The research was simulation. The benchmarks were FAIR.
doe-osti-3012635-carbon-capture-pilot-at: Vicksburg mill got carbon-piloted, and this DOE final covers the containerboard capture. The pages detail the technical findings. The industry folks get their closeout. The mill was containerboard. The closeout was industry. The capture was carbon. The pilot was capture.
doe-osti-3021453-scalable-ai-optimizatio: X-ScaleAI got DeepHyper-integrated, and this DOE final optimizes scalable AI. The pages detail the report findings. The computing folks get their closeout. The optimization was scalable. The closeout was computing. The AI was scalable. The DeepHyper was integration.
doe-osti-3376725-criteria-for-retention-: 3013 S1 got retention-criteriad, and this DOE text covers container risk. The pages detail the relative findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The judgment was expert. The data were nuclear. The containers were S1. The risk were relative. The judgment were expert.
doe-osti-3384923-crada-number-nfe-22-093: Captis Aire got CRADA-finalled, and this DOE NFE-22-09315 covers the LLC. The pages detail the report findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was energy. The Captis were Aire. The LLC were final.
doe-osti-3995273-evaluation-of-artificia: A bill of materials lists every part in a product — thousands of lines to check. Roth and colleagues evaluate AI and machine learning approaches for analyzing BOMs. The evaluation shows where the algorithms help and where human experts still win.
froudacity-west-indian-fables-by-james-a:
J. J. Thomas's Froudacity, printed in 1889, answers James Anthony Froude's travel book on the British West Indies point by point. Thomas, a Trinidad schoolmaster and scholar, read Froude in Grenada and saw, under the rhetorical flowers, a scheme to deny the colonies elected legislatures. Froude argued that the islands' African majority made self-government a menace to civilization. Thomas's preface names that argument plainly and promises to dismantle it with Froude's own pages.

Inside, the four books follow Froude island by island: Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, then Trinidad at length. Thomas corrects scenes, statistics, and portraits of Black workers, clergy, and voters as he goes. A historical summary closes the case for West Indian capacity and confederation. Readers get a landmark of Caribbean letters, a colonial subject writing back to a famous historian in his own language, and winning the argument on evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierWBCaptai:
Dallas Police Captain W. B. Frazier gave the FBI a set of statements about a dangerous duty. His subject was the threats made against prisoner Lee Harvey Oswald and the security planned for Oswald's transfer on November 24, 1963. That transfer is the one Jack Ruby broke through to shoot Oswald on live television.

After Ruby's shot, every security decision was re-examined. The captain who helped arrange the move had to explain the threats he knew of and the precautions taken. His statements preserve the police account of a failure that happened in front of the whole country.
narrative-of-the-voyages-round-the-world:
Andrew Kippis tells the life and voyages of Captain James Cook here. Kippis dedicates the book to the King with high praise. Royal bounty, he says, made Cook's vast undertakings possible. Without it, the world would lack vast new light on geography.

Cook's three voyages round the world form the book's core. Kippis also covers Cook's life between and before the voyages. He credits the King's support of science for an age of knowledge. The narrative made Cook's fame plain to common readers. It stands as an early, full life of the navigator who redrew the Pacific map.
nasa-tm-19660017562-some-results-concern:
Edith I Reed at Goddard and Jacques E Blamont of the national research center in Paris reported results on the airglow as seen from the OGO-II satellite. Airglow is a faint light the upper air gives off at all hours. Its main spectral lines carry facts about the gases that emit them. A corrected copy of the paper is dated 1966 in the sample.

Measuring airglow from a satellite avoids the glow's being drowned by ground lights and haze. Each line points to a certain gas at a certain height. Reed and Blamont present some results on those principal lines. International teamwork on a United States satellite was itself a mark of the era's space science.
nasa-tm-19700022586-experimental-evaluat:
Edward R. Furman of the Lewis Research Center led this study, with Robert D. Brooks and R. W. Harrison of the General Electric Company in Cincinnati. Their paper was written for a 1970 energy conversion conference in Las Vegas. It evaluates mercury boilers for the SNAP-8 power system.

The boilers were built from tantalum joined to stainless steel. In the SNAP-8 design, a boiler turns liquid mercury into vapor that drives a turbine. Tests judged how well these boilers worked and held up. SNAP-8 was a nuclear power system meant to supply electricity on long space missions.
nasa-tm-19710017498-a-reference-atmosphe:
E A Carter and S C Brown of the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this reference on May 10, 1971, as NASA TM X-64590. Both worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. The book gives a standard atmosphere for Vandenberg Air Force Base in California. This is the annual version for 1971. Launch teams on the West Coast used Vandenberg for polar orbit missions.

A reference atmosphere lists expected air values by height. The tables cover heat, pressure, and density through the air column. Engineers feed those values into flight and reentry calculations. A shared standard keeps every team's math on the same footing. The catalog record notes the tables rest on a current annual tabulation.
nasa-tm-19710079289-an-investigation-of-:
Raymond M. Hicks, Joel P. Mendoza, and Lionel L. Levy Jr. of the Ames Research Center wrote this investigation, NASA TM X-62,030, on sonic booms from returning space shuttle orbiters. A reentering orbiter drags a boom carpet across the ground below its flight path. Planners needed to know how strong that boom would be before choosing an orbiter shape.

Wind tunnel tests measured boom overpressure for two shapes: a straight-wing orbiter and a delta-wing orbiter. Two reentry trajectories were analyzed for the delta design and one for the straight wing. The authors found that trajectory and angle of attack both strongly affect the boom level under the flight path. A gentler, constant angle of attack for the delta orbiter kept the overpressure low. It stayed under about one pound per square foot across the speeds tested.
tanakh-jps-1917-haggai:
Haggai is a brief prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English of the Jewish Publication Society. Its words are dated to the second year of Darius the king and sent to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and Joshua the high priest.

The charge is plain: the people live in fine roofed houses while God's house still lies in ruins. Their fields yield little, their pay leaks away like coins in a holed bag, and rain is held back. Haggai urges them to haul wood from the hills and build. Readers get a short, sharp call to put shared worship first after exile, with drought read as a sign of misplaced care.
the-hawaiian-romance-of-laieikawai: Martha Warren Beckwith supplied the introduction and translation for The Hawaiian Romance of Laieikawai. The contents list study sections on the persons, action, and background of the story, followed by the text and translation in twenty-seven chapters. Chapter titles trace the birth of the Princess, her flight to Paliuli, suitors who seek her, a boxing match with Cold-nose, and a journey to the Heavens. Front matter is all that is present here.
the-scouts-of-stonewall-the-story-of-the:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Scouts of Stonewall retells the great Valley campaign as a story. His foreword calls it an independent story. In effect, though, it continues a series. That series began with The Guns of Bull Run and went on with The Guns of Shiloh. This romance returns to the Southern side, Altsheler says.

The book follows Harry Kenton and his friends. A character list introduces Harry as a lad fighting for the South. His cousin Dick Mason fights for the North. Colonel George Kenton is Harry's father. Colonel Leonidas Talbot commands the Invincibles, a Southern regiment. Lieutenant Colonel Hector St. Hilaire is his second in command. Other figures include a Northern spy, William J. Shepard. A Vermont youth who loves mathematics, George Warner, also appears.
